source: Use exact proposed literals already preserved in original payload plus v2 and final Escape correction; no literal/hash replacement in this mapping.

explanation.sourceRationale: The saved source defines escape speed as the minimum initial speed and derives the threshold by setting speed to zero at infinity.
explanation.editorialRationale: The explanation applies that minimum-energy definition to the Earth-surface, no-atmosphere value in the stem.

answers[0].note.sourceRationale: The source definition directly supports the keyed 11.2 km/s value as the minimum Earth escape speed in the stated idealization.
answers[0].note.editorialRationale: This note identifies why the keyed value satisfies the minimum-speed condition.

answers[1].note.sourceRationale: The source defines the needed initial speed as a minimum threshold; a value below that threshold does not meet it.
answers[1].note.editorialRationale: This note explains the 7.9 km/s distractor as below the required Earth escape threshold.

answers[2].note.sourceRationale: The same minimum-threshold definition supports rejecting a 1.1 km/s launch speed for Earth.
answers[2].note.editorialRationale: This note gives the physical reason the 1.1 km/s choice fails, with no unsourced comparisons to other bodies.

answers[3].note.sourceRationale: The source asks for the minimum initial speed; a speed above the threshold is not the minimum requested.
answers[3].note.editorialRationale: This note explains why 29.8 km/s may exceed the threshold but does not answer the minimum-value question.

explanation.sourceRationale: The saved §17.4 passage connects source approach with shorter forward wavelength and higher received frequency.
explanation.editorialRationale: The explanation traces the stem’s approach condition through wavefront spacing to the observed frequency.

answers[0].note.sourceRationale: The source states that the observer ahead of an approaching source receives shorter-spaced fronts and higher frequency.
answers[0].note.editorialRationale: This note supports the keyed higher-frequency response for the stated approach.

answers[1].note.sourceRationale: The source associates lower frequency with the receding side, not the approaching side.
answers[1].note.editorialRationale: This note identifies the direction reversal in the lower-frequency distractor.

answers[2].note.sourceRationale: The source describes a change in frequency from changed wavefront spacing; it does not describe the periodic wave as disappearing.
answers[2].note.editorialRationale: This note explains why zero frequency is not the result of approach.

answers[3].note.sourceRationale: The source attributes frequency shift to relative source-observer motion, which this stem specifies.
answers[3].note.editorialRationale: This note points out that unchanged frequency would miss the given approach condition.

explanation.sourceRationale: The saved §31.5 paragraph enumerates N/2 after one interval and N/4 after the next.
explanation.editorialRationale: The explanation shows both successive halvings needed for the keyed quarter.

answers[0].note.sourceRationale: The source says half of the remaining nuclei decay in each half-life.
answers[0].note.editorialRationale: This note states the repeated operation underlying the keyed one-quarter result.

answers[1].note.sourceRationale: The source lists one-eighth after three successive halvings, whereas the stem gives two periods.
answers[1].note.editorialRationale: This note ties the one-eighth distractor to the extra interval it would require.

answers[2].note.sourceRationale: Repeated division of the surviving amount by two does not produce one-third after two periods.
answers[2].note.editorialRationale: This note distinguishes repeated halving from a one-third decrement.

answers[3].note.sourceRationale: The source gives one-half after the first period and then halves the remainder in the next.
answers[3].note.editorialRationale: This note explains that the half-only distractor stops after one of the two requested periods.

explanation.sourceRationale: The saved §12.3 passage states total entropy in a spontaneous process increases or remains constant, never decreases.
explanation.editorialRationale: The explanation maps this rule to reversible constancy and irreversible increase for the isolated system.

answers[0].note.sourceRationale: The source explicitly rules out decrease of total entropy in a spontaneous process.
answers[0].note.editorialRationale: This note directly rejects the decrease option for the system specified.

answers[1].note.sourceRationale: The source permits both increase and equality, which together mean nondecrease.
answers[1].note.editorialRationale: This note explains why the keyed wording is more accurate than strict increase.

answers[2].note.sourceRationale: The saved second-law passage concerns the direction of entropy change, not a universal zero value.
answers[2].note.editorialRationale: This note rejects strict zero without invoking an unsupported third-law claim.

answers[3].note.sourceRationale: The source gives a monotonic nondecrease condition, not periodic sign changes.
answers[3].note.editorialRationale: This note explains why periodic sign reversal is unrelated to the rule being tested.

explanation.sourceRationale: The saved §23.1 text says changing magnetic flux induces EMF and that EMF may exist without a current path.
explanation.editorialRationale: The explanation separates the induced voltage from the current that the open switch prevents.

answers[0].note.sourceRationale: The source permits EMF without current; an open path blocks the asserted current.
answers[0].note.editorialRationale: This note addresses both halves of the false option in their stated order.

answers[1].note.sourceRationale: Changing flux creates EMF, while the source separately requires a current path for current flow.
answers[1].note.editorialRationale: This note supports the keyed combination of induced EMF and no current through the open switch.

answers[2].note.sourceRationale: The source explicitly allows induced EMF without a current path.
answers[2].note.editorialRationale: This note rejects the claim that opening the switch prevents EMF itself.

answers[3].note.sourceRationale: The source identifies change in magnetic flux as the condition for induced EMF.
answers[3].note.editorialRationale: This note corrects the option’s reversal from changing to constant flux.

explanation.sourceRationale: The saved §25.4 paragraph requires a lower-index second medium and incidence above the critical angle.
explanation.editorialRationale: The explanation keeps both necessary conditions together so neither is mistaken as sufficient alone.

answers[0].note.sourceRationale: The source requires an incident angle above critical; normal incidence does not meet that condition.
answers[0].note.editorialRationale: This note is specific to the perpendicular-incidence distractor.

answers[1].note.sourceRationale: The source states n1>n2 and incidence angle greater than critical.
answers[1].note.editorialRationale: This note corresponds to the keyed pair of conditions; the answer literal uses a decoded literal greater-than sign.

answers[2].note.sourceRationale: The source requires the second medium’s refractive index to be lower than the first.
answers[2].note.editorialRationale: This note identifies that travel from vacuum into a higher-index medium reverses the required direction.

answers[3].note.sourceRationale: Equal indices do not satisfy the required decrease from n1 to n2.
answers[3].note.editorialRationale: This note explains the equal-index distractor using the source’s index-order condition.

explanation.sourceRationale: The saved §13.1 passage identifies 0 K as the lowest possible temperature and gives −273.15 °C.
explanation.editorialRationale: The explanation states the scale correspondence without adding a claim about microscopic motion.

answers[0].note.sourceRationale: Using the source Kelvin-Celsius offset, −100 °C remains about 173 K above zero kelvin.
answers[0].note.editorialRationale: This note relates the −100 °C distractor to the absolute-zero reference.

answers[1].note.sourceRationale: The source explicitly gives −273.15 °C as the Celsius coordinate of 0 K.
answers[1].note.editorialRationale: This note directly supports the keyed value.

answers[2].note.sourceRationale: Applying the source offset to −173 °C gives approximately 100 K.
answers[2].note.editorialRationale: This note explains the shifted-temperature distractor with its corresponding Kelvin value.

answers[3].note.sourceRationale: The source distinguishes 0 K from ordinary Celsius reference temperatures.
answers[3].note.editorialRationale: This note separates water’s 0 °C freezing point from absolute zero.

explanation.sourceRationale: The saved §8.3 passage states total momentum is conserved for an isolated system and distinguishes inelastic kinetic-energy loss.
explanation.editorialRationale: The explanation addresses the system sum and avoids implying every collision conserves kinetic energy.

answers[0].note.sourceRationale: The source defines total momentum as the sum of individual momenta, not an invariant for each body.
answers[0].note.editorialRationale: This note addresses the individual-body-momentum distractor.

answers[1].note.sourceRationale: The source’s isolated-system relation equates total momentum before and after.
answers[1].note.editorialRationale: This note directly supports the keyed system-total quantity.

answers[2].note.sourceRationale: The source states kinetic energy can change in an inelastic collision.
answers[2].note.editorialRationale: This note explains why kinetic energy is not conserved in every collision.

answers[3].note.sourceRationale: The source’s sticking-together example is a special case; momentum conservation does not require all collisions to end with equal speeds.
answers[3].note.editorialRationale: This note rejects the distractor’s universal equal-speed claim while leaving the key untouched.
